title: Humanoid Robots Are Entering the Workforce

slides.heading: Humanoid Robots Are Entering the Workforce
slides.body: From factory floors to fulfillment centers — the robot coworker era has begun

slides.heading: What Is a Humanoid Robot?
slides.body: Humanoid robots have a human-like body — two arms, two legs, and a torso. This shape lets them use existing tools and spaces built for people, making them versatile in real-world environments without costly redesigns.

slides.heading: The Race to Deploy
slides.body: By 2026, companies like Tesla (Optimus), Figure AI, and Agility Robotics (Digit) have moved beyond prototypes. Hundreds of units are now operating in warehouses, car plants, and logistics centers across the US and Asia.

slides.heading: How They Learn to Work
slides.body: Modern humanoids learn through imitation — watching humans perform tasks thousands of times. AI models then let robots generalize those movements to new objects and situations, without manual programming for each scenario.

slides.heading: What Jobs Are They Doing?
slides.body: Current deployments focus on repetitive, physically demanding work: moving boxes, sorting packages, and assembling parts. These roles have high injury rates and chronic staffing shortages, making them ideal first targets.

slides.heading: The Economics of Robot Labor
slides.body: A humanoid robot costs roughly $20,000–$50,000 today, with a target of under $15,000 by 2027. At those prices, leasing a robot is cheaper than a full-time minimum-wage worker within 18 months of deployment.

slides.heading: Key Technical Challenges
slides.body: Robots still struggle with dexterous hand manipulation, unpredictable environments, and battery life (typically 4–8 hours). Stairs and cluttered spaces remain difficult. Reliability in real-world conditions is the #1 barrier to mass adoption.

slides.heading: Impact on Human Workers
slides.body: Economists estimate humanoids could automate 10–20% of physical jobs by 2030. Most experts predict a shift rather than elimination — humans moving to supervision, maintenance, and edge-case handling roles as robots handle routine tasks.

slides.heading: The Road to 1 Million Robots
slides.body: Major manufacturers are targeting production at scale: Tesla aims for millions of Optimus units by 2030. If achieved, it would be the fastest scaling of any new technology category in history — surpassing even smartphones.

slides.heading: The Future Is Already on the Floor
slides.body: Humanoid robots won't replace human creativity or judgment anytime soon — but they're already changing how physical work gets done. The question isn't if, but how fast the transition will reshape every industry that relies on human hands.
